title: Lords of the Dance: Professionals as Institutional Agents
author: W. Richard Scott

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field
st.an: Scott accepts the cluster’s framing of professional authority as institutionally constructed rather than reducible to technical expertise. He materially extends it by treating professionals as creators and appliers of governing frameworks, recommending field-level analysis, and distinguishing expertise-based authority from authority grounded in coercive or monetary resources.
qs: By this, I mean that their primary social function can be described as variously specializing in creating, testing, conveying, and applying cultural-cognitive, normative, and/or regulative frameworks that govern one or another social sphere.

Although members of the police, the army or corporate management claim to       possess specialized expertise, their ultimate authority rests on their legitimate       access to coercive powers, such as the use of weapons or incarceration, or to the       control of monetary resources.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Scott supports the core view that technology and codification conditionally supplement, displace and redistribute professional tasks rather than producing inevitable wholesale replacement. He materially extends the cluster by locating work redesign within broader organizational, market and managerial transformations, though he does not address AI-specific jagged capability or verification.
qs: Such efforts can supplement,       but can also undermine or replace the judgments of individual clinicians.

Change in the Nature of Clients As organizations have grown in size and influence, many existing professions were motivated (or obliged) to change the nature of their practice to accommodate the interests of a new type of client: the collective or corporate actor.

st.t: Elite renewal: Innovation can reproduce legal power
st.an: Scott supports the cluster’s core account of professional authority as grounded in provider interests, occupational competition, political power and historically variable state–society relations rather than technical expertise alone. The excerpt does not itself develop the stronger claim that legal innovation renews elite power, but it directly supplies the broader political-professional framework on which that claim rests.
qs: status and the obvious rewards — money, status, influence — accruing to win-       ners, these critics refocused the debate, shifting attention from clients’ to       providers’ interests and from technical or knowledge-based claims to political       explanations.

kp.d: Scott's central theoretical thesis is that professions are modern society's leading institutional agents: they create, interpret and apply frameworks governing social activity. This 2008 article supplies historical and theoretical analysis of professional change, rather than evidence about AI adoption or its effects.
qs: Professionals are not the only, but are — I believe — the most influential, contemporary crafters of institutions.
And, it is primarily the professions that build and tend these systems.

kp.k: Institutional theory bridges functionalist and conflict accounts
kp.d: Scott contrasts functionalist accounts emphasizing knowledge, autonomy and service with conflict accounts emphasizing monopoly, occupational competition and political power. His proposed social-constructionist account allows knowledge claims to be sincere yet partly arbitrary, jurisdictions to change without being reducible to political power, and professional interests to coexist with client welfare. This is a theoretical reconciliation, not a tested causal finding.
qs: The tensions between the functionalist and the conflict models have not been completely resolved, but more recent efforts have attempted to accommodate insights from both perspectives.
the knowledge claims advanced by professionals can be both somewhat arbitrary and sincerely advanced

kp.k: Institutional agency need not mean deliberate self-interest
kp.d: Scott qualifies the contrast between institutions emerging through collective sense-making and institutions intentionally constructed through power. Drawing on Emirbayer and Mische, Meyer, and Pierson, he argues that agency encompasses routine reproduction and creativity, may serve others or collective goods, and can generate unintended consequences or fail as conditions and interests change.
qs: This distinction between more or less conscious and intentional institutional construction is no doubt overdrawn.
social agency can be employed in the ser- vice of self-interest, service to other actors, or on behalf of ‘nonactor entities recognized in the cultural system’

kp.k: Professional authority rests on three distinct institutional pillars
kp.d: Scott distinguishes cultural-cognitive authority through knowledge and shared interpretive frameworks, normative authority through prescriptions and obligations, and regulative authority through rules and sanctions. Professions emphasize different combinations of these mechanisms; authority is therefore not reducible to either expertise or coercion alone.
qs: the regulative pillar, which stresses rule-setting, monitoring and sanctioning activities, both formal and informal;
There exist multiple vocabularies of control and multiple modes of legitimating professional authority.

kp.k: Knowledge professions govern through shared understandings
kp.d: In Scott's cultural-cognitive category, professionals shape how problems, methods and solutions are understood. Drawing on Knorr-Certina and Starr, he distinguishes internal control through shared conceptions of work from external cultural authority, which depends on clients accepting professional knowledge claims and believing those claims are used on their behalf.
qs: The primary weapon of many professions is ideas.
Work is governed by common understandings of ‘the substance of the work’
the client accepts the knowledge claims made by the professional and believes that they are being employed on the client’s behalf.

kp.k: Expert standards extend governance beyond coercive law
kp.d: Scott describes professional associations and international nongovernmental organizations as increasingly transnational standard setters, particularly since World War II. Reporting Brunsson and Jacobsson and related scholarship, he explains that these bodies seek compliance through claims of scientific superiority, adopter benefit or humanity's long-term interests rather than coercion or financial inducements. The article also notes public ambivalence toward science and expertise.
qs: Such bodies lack the coercive powers exercised by states or corporations
‘soft’ rules — standards and guidelines — rather than ‘hard’ legal frameworks backed by sanctions

kp.k: State backing supports professional jurisdiction and coercive authority
kp.d: Scott identifies legal professionals in legislatures and courts, military and police personnel, and managerial professionals as occupations with privileged access to regulatory powers. More broadly, state backing can protect professional entry conditions, jurisdictions and practice rights. He stresses variation across societies and distinguishes specialized expertise from legitimate control over penalties, rewards and resources.
qs: Some professions have privileged access to the use of regulatory powers.
It is here that the power to control rewards and penalties looms large.

kp.k: Institutional innovation spans creative, carrier and clinical roles
kp.d: Scott proposes three professional roles: a relatively small creative group develops and warrants frameworks; carriers such as educators, lawyers and consultants diffuse and translate them; and clinicians, comprising the largest proportion, apply principles to particular problems. Carriers and experienced clinicians also innovate through adaptation, so institutional creation is not confined to researchers. He identifies accumulated court decisions as a visible instance of this broader process.
qs: creative professionals, carrier professionals, and clinical professionals.
carriers are responsible for substantial innovation and creative adaptation in the messages they carry.
this task, in varying degrees, is widely shared throughout the full spectrum of professional roles.

kp.k: Specialization can fragment collective professional power
kp.d: Using US medicine and Scott et al. (2000), Scott reports no formally recognized physician specialties in 1900, the first in 1917, and, at the article's contemporary reference point, more than 25 board-certified specialty categories encompassing over 125 sub-specialties, with well over 80% of practicing physicians qualified as specialists. He links specialization to fragmented knowledge and interests. AMA membership fell from over 80% of practicing physicians during the 1950s to fewer than 40% at the reported present, while specialist associations expanded; Scott argues this diminished medicine's collective policy influence.
qs: The first such specialty was cre- ated in 1917.
The profession of medicine no longer speaks with a unified voice.

kp.k: Professional expansion diversifies roles and subordinate occupations
kp.d: Scott describes growth in teaching, research, consultancy, management and policy roles as knowledge systems expand, with a higher proportion of professionals working outside direct client practice. In medicine, he also describes parallel and subordinate occupations and reports more than 40 officially certified health occupations in California, citing Scott et al. (2000). These occupational arrangements remain shaped by medical authority and jurisdictional competition.
qs: I term this the growth of the ‘hyphenated professional’.
There are teaching physicians, research physicians, consultant physicians and manager physicians.

kp.k: Mechanization and codification can replace professional judgment
kp.d: Scott argues that expanding knowledge enables both specialization and the mechanization, routinization and commodification of work. Drawing on technology and labor scholarship, he notes that machines operated by less-skilled workers can replace expert skills. Consolidating and formalizing knowledge also produces computer-aided diagnosis, decision protocols and self-care manuals, which may supplement, undermine or replace clinicians' judgments. These are general historical mechanisms, not findings about generative AI.
qs: Subdivision of work is associated not only with the development of higher levels of specialization and greater expertise, but also with the possibility of mechanization.
Such efforts can supplement,       but can also undermine or replace the judgments of individual clinicians.

kp.k: Corporate clients reshape professional markets and organizations
kp.d: Scott argues that increasingly powerful organizational clients changed accounting, architecture and law. Professionals serving corporate clients became higher-status and better-paid segments, while organizational demand encouraged group practices and firms. Multinational clients subsequently encouraged multidisciplinary service provision, producing larger, more differentiated and more corporate-like professional organizations.
qs: many existing professions were motivated (or obliged) to change the nature of their practice to accommodate the interests of a new type of client: the collective or corporate actor.
there is a relatively clear division between pro- fessionals who service individual, and those who work for corporate, clients.

kp.k: Managed businesses increasingly displace collegial partnership structures
kp.d: Citing a decade-long University of Alberta research program, Scott describes a shift from professional partnership governance toward managed professional businesses. Strategic planning, marketing, coordination and managerial integration gain priority over informal collegial autonomy. Managers need not belong to the profession they manage, and traditional professionals increasingly seek management education to retain organizational control.
qs: ‘col- legiality, peer evaluation, autonomy, informality, and flexibility of structure’
managers who may or may not themselves be members of the particular professional group being managed
More and more engineers, physicians, and lawyers are seeking MBA degrees to augment their specialized training.

kp.k: Market legitimacy challenges professional social trusteeship
kp.d: Drawing particularly on Brint, Scott argues that twentieth-century professional change, accelerated by neoliberal doctrine, shifted legitimacy from civic-minded social trusteeship toward technical expertise validated by markets. He associates this shift with privatization, for-profit enterprises, managerial controls and narrower service commitments. The argument concerns changing professional institutional models over time and place, rather than an invariant definition of professionalism.
qs: the market is viewed as the ultimate arbiter of social value.
It is important that we recognize that the occupations we code as professions vary from time to time and place to place.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Scott makes no explicit AI claim. His relevant cross-domain claims concern mechanization and the formalization of professional knowledge, illustrated principally through medicine.
pts.d: Scott argues that machinery can transfer formerly expert tasks to semiskilled technicians, replacing rather than necessarily enhancing professional skill. He also argues that consolidating and codifying knowledge can produce computer-aided diagnosis, decision protocols and self-care manuals that supplement, undermine or replace individual clinical judgment. These are claims about technology and professional work generally, not predictions about generative AI or AI-driven legal services.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The relevant claims rest on a theoretical synthesis, cited scholarship and illustrative mechanisms, not an AI evaluation or a quantified technology-impact study.
pts.d: In the mechanization discussion on page 230, Scott cites Zuboff (1988) in connection with replacement of human skill and Braverman (1974) in connection with deskilling. His discussion of knowledge formalization identifies computer-aided diagnosis, practitioner protocols and self-care manuals as examples, without presenting measured effects or a separate empirical test. Elsewhere, he supplies historical statistics about medical specialization, but those figures do not measure technological substitution.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims describe historical developments and possibilities already present when the article appeared in 2008; they do not specify a future AI adoption timetable.
pts.d: Scott situates these mechanisms within endogenous changes arising from the growth and subdivision of professional knowledge. Mechanization becomes possible as work is subdivided; formalization can either support or displace judgment. His qualifications—some tasks, the possibility of mechanization, and effects that can supplement or replace—do not assert inevitable replacement of whole professions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are expert practitioners, individual clinicians, semiskilled technicians and paraprofessionals.
pts.d: In Scott's account, some tasks previously requiring expert dexterity become machine-mediated work performed by semiskilled technicians. Clinicians may gain decision support or find their judgment undermined or replaced by codified knowledge. The surrounding illustration concerns US medicine, although Scott presents the mechanisms as relevant to professional work more broadly. He does not establish corresponding effects on lawyers, law-firm staffing, legal prices or legal clients.
